To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ERG and the spike discharge are affected reversibly by the variations in the flow rate, temperature, osmolarity, pH and O2, glucose and phosphate contents in the perfusates.

(1) the ERG and the spike discharge are maintained for at least 6 hr when the isolated carp retina is perfused with a standard balanced salt solution, keeping the flow rate at about 2 ml/min, the temperature at 25°C and the pH at 7·5–8·0, (2) the ERG is linearly related to the perfusate flow rate in the range of about 0·5–3·0 ml/min, (3) the

the isolated carp retina is capable of maintaining a constant physiological state for more than 5 hr under the standard conditions of perfusion, and that the retinal activities are sensitive to the changes in the perfusates, especially in osmotic pressure, temperature, pH and O2, and to a lesser degree, in glucose concentration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of variations of biophysical and biochemical conditions in the perfusates on the ERG, and the spike discharging of identified ganglion cell.
the optimal conditions of perfusion for the isolated carp retina and with the effects of variations of the perfusates on the ERG of the carp retina and spike discharges.
the effect of variations in the composition and the physical conditions of the perfusating solution on the electrical activities of the carp retina.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the optimal condition for maintaining a steady retinal activity is as follows: perfusion with a balanced salt solution at 2·5 ml/min flow rate, 20°C temperature, 7·0–8·0 pH, and 100–120 mosmol osmotic pressure.

the ERG and the discharge of ganglion cell were most stable in a balanced salt solution with the pH adjusted to 8·0, the temperature to 20°C, the flow rate to 2·0–4·0 ml/min, and with the presence of O2 and glucose in the perfusates.

the isolated carp retina can be maintained in a steady physiological state for a long time by perfusing it with a standard solution at a pH of 8·0, a temperature of 25–28°C and a flow rate of 2·0–4·0 ml/min, and by keeping the O2 and glucose concentration at 100% and 1·0–1·5 mg/ml, respectively.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in order to keep the isolated carp retina in a steady state, the following conditions should be satisfied: the perfusion flow rate should be maintained at more than 1·0 ml/min, the temperature at 22–26°C, the osmotic pressure between 250 and 300 mosmol, the pH at 7·8–8·2 and the O2 concentration at more than 50% in the perfusates.
the ERG and ganglion cell discharges in the isolated carp eye can be maintained for more than six hours by perfusing the eye with a balanced salt solution at a temperature of 20–25°C and a pH of 8·0.

the ERG and ganglion-cell discharges are sensitive to changes in perfusate flow rate, temperature, osmotic pressure and pH, but are insensitive to changes in the concentrations of Na+, K+, Ca++, Mg++, Cl−, HCO3−, H2PO4−, glucose and amino acids.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the isolated carp retina can be maintained in a healthy physiological condition for a long time (more than 6 hr) by using the standard perfusate with pH 8·0, flow rate 2·0ml/min, temperature 20°C and O2 saturation.

the isolated carp retina is very stable in terms of the ERG and the discharge of ganglion cell, and that the retinal activities can be maintained at a constant level over several hours if the perfusate has the proper composition and is supplied at the proper flow rate.

the perfusion of the isolated carp retina with a balanced salt solution, saturated with a gas mixture containing 97% O and 3%CO2, and at a flow rate of 2·0–2·5 ml/min and a temperature of 20–25°C is the optimal condition for maintaining the physiological state of the retina for more than 5 hr.
